hook.text: On a hundred items, almost any code is fast. The interview question is what it costs at a million, and which structure keeps it cheap.

plan.text: Thirty-five questions, argued with counts, not code: eight with a figure each, three inside those, and twenty-four quickly.

big.text: Question one. What is Big-O notation, and why do interviewers care? It says how time or memory grows with the input size, n, ignoring constants.

big-count.text: A double loop over a hundred items checks under five thousand pairs. Instant.

big-million.text: At a million items, it's half a trillion.

big-model.text: Model it at a hundred million checks a second, an assumption: about eighty-three minutes. One pass over the million: a hundredth of a second.

big-why.text: That's why they care: Big-O predicts whether a solution survives its real input. The usual game is turning a brute-force n squared into n.

big-next.text: But constants are dropped, so at a hundred items the brute force is often fine, and simpler. Say what it costs, and where it stops being fine.

hash.text: Question two. When do you reach for a hash map? When you need lookups and inserts by key in constant time on average: counting, grouping, have I seen this?

hash-twosum.text: It turns Two Sum's double loop into one pass: at each number, ask the map for target minus it, then store the number. Linear time, at the cost of linear memory.

hash-collide.text: Average is the key word. With a thousand buckets, a shared bucket is more likely than not by the thirty-eighth key.

hash-worst.text: The follow-up is the worst case. Give a thousand keys the same hash, and filling a Python set takes nearly six hundred thousand key comparisons. With distinct hashes, none.

hash-set.text: That's a hash set: constant on average, linear space, and linear per operation at worst.

amort.text: Question three. What is amortized O of one, and when does it apply? It spreads a rare expensive step's cost over the cheap ones around it.

amort-run.text: Append a million items to a Python list. It runs out of room eighty-six times, and each move to a bigger block can copy every item so far.

amort-total.text: Add those copies up: about eight copies per append, at any length. Constant, on average.

amort-factor.text: A textbook array doubles, for under two copies an append. Python grows by about an eighth, so it copies more often. Any fixed factor keeps it constant, a hash table's rehash too.

amort-spike.text: But that's an average, not a promise per call: the append that triggers the last resize can copy nine hundred thirty-nine thousand items. On a latency budget, allocate up front.

stack.text: Question four. When is a stack the right structure? When the problem is about the most recent thing still open: nesting, undo, backtracking. Last in, first out.

stack-count.text: A counter can't do it. This string opens and closes one round and one square bracket, so counting accepts it. But the round one closes while the square one inside is open.

stack-run.text: A stack keeps the openers, newest on top, and each closer must match the top: rejected.

stack-queue.text: A queue matches the oldest opener instead, so it gets both wrong: it accepts this one, and rejects a correctly nested string.

stack-next.text: Depth-first search is the same idea: the path you're on is the stack.

bfs.text: Question five. Walk me through BFS versus DFS: when do you choose each? Breadth-first search takes a queue, level by level. Depth-first takes a stack and follows one path down.

bfs-graph.text: Node A leads to B and C, and both lead to D. Breadth-first visits A, B, C, D; depth-first, A, B, D, then C.

bfs-short.text: Choose BFS for shortest paths in an unweighted graph: it reaches each node first by the fewest edges. DFS for cycle detection, topological sort and backtracking.

bfs-memory.text: Memory decides it too. On a full binary tree of a million nodes, BFS holds the widest level, five hundred twenty-four thousand nodes; DFS holds one path, twenty.

bfs-deque.text: And make the queue a deque, a double-ended queue. Popping a Python list's front shifts everything behind it: two hundred seventy-five billion moves here. A deque pops either end in constant time.
bfs-deque.spoken: And make the queue a deck, a double-ended queue. Popping a Python list's front shifts everything behind it: two hundred seventy-five billion moves here. A deck pops either end in constant time.

pq.text: Question six. How does a priority queue differ from a regular queue? A queue serves in arrival order. A priority queue serves the most urgent first, as in a scheduler or Dijkstra's algorithm.

heap-choose.text: Keep a list sorted, most urgent at the end, and a pop is instant, but at a million items an insert shifts half a million on average. An unsorted list inserts instantly and scans to pop.

heap-height.text: A heap does both in log n, each parent at least as urgent as its children. A million items make twenty levels, so a push or pop moves at most nineteen; a peek is constant.

heap-build.text: The follow-up: building a heap is linear, not n log n, since most nodes sit near the bottom. For a million items arriving least urgent first, heapify takes one and a half million comparisons; pushed one at a time, eighteen million.

dijk.text: Question seven. Explain Dijkstra's algorithm and its complexity. It finds shortest paths from one source when no weight is negative, a min-heap handing out the closest unfinished node next.

dijk-run.text: C costs four directly but three through B. D costs four, through B and C.

dijk-cost.text: With V nodes and E edges, each node is finished once, and each edge can cost a heap push of log V: V plus E, times log V.

dijk-neg.text: Why no negative weights? A node is final when it leaves the heap. B leaves at two, and only later does the minus-two edge from C reach it at one. B is wrong, and so is D.

dijk-bf.text: Bellman-Ford instead tries every edge V minus one times: V times E, slower, and right.

quick.text: Question eight. How does quicksort work, and what is its worst case? Pick a pivot, split the rest into smaller and larger, and sort each side. On average, n log n.

quick-sorted.text: The worst case is n squared, when the pivot is always the smallest or largest. Pivot a thousand sorted numbers on the last, and each split peels off one: half a million comparisons, nearly a thousand levels.

quick-limit.text: Written recursively, that's past Python's default limit.

quick-random.text: Random pivots on the same input: eleven thousand comparisons, twenty-one levels.

quick-next.text: And sorted input is common, rows by ID or events by time, so randomize. Quicksort's edge over merge sort is sorting in place.

rapid-in.text: The other twenty-four, one line each. Sorting first.

r-merge.text: Merge sort halves, sorts each half and merges in linear time: n log n always, stable, with linear extra memory. Python's sort builds on it.

r-heapsort.text: Heapsort guarantees n log n in constant extra space, but is less cache-friendly than quicksort. It suits tight memory.

r-stable.text: A stable sort keeps ties in order. Sort by first name, then stable-sort by last, and the two Hoppers stay in first-name order.

r-inplace.text: In place means constant extra memory, or log n of stack: quicksort, with random pivots. Out of place grows with the input: merge sort.

r-master.text: The Master Theorem solves divide-and-conquer recurrences by comparing the work of combining with the number of smallest pieces. For merge sort they tie, so n log n.

r-recursion.text: Recursion fits trees, but every call takes a stack frame, and Python stops at a thousand. A loop with an explicit stack avoids that.

r-dc.text: Divide and conquer splits into independent subproblems, like merge sort. Dynamic programming reuses the answers of overlapping ones.

r-memo.text: Memoization recurses and caches, top-down. Tabulation fills a table bottom-up. Naive Fibonacci of thirty makes two point seven million calls; memoized, fifty-nine.

r-classic.text: Know coin change, longest common subsequence, knapsack, edit distance and word break: each teaches a way to define the state.

r-greedy.text: Greedy takes the best-looking step, safe only when local choices provably add up. To make six from coins of one, three and four, it takes three coins. Two threes do it.

r-backtrack.text: Backtracking builds a candidate step by step and drops a branch the moment it can't succeed: N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations.

r-array.text: An array indexes in constant time and caches well, but a middle insert shifts the rest. A linked list splices in constant time given the node; finding it is a walk.

r-bst.text: A binary search tree, or BST, costs its height per operation. A thousand keys inserted in order stand a thousand levels tall; shuffled, twenty-one. AVL and red-black trees stay at log n.

r-traverse.text: In-order traversal visits a BST in sorted order. Pre-order, root first, serializes a tree. Post-order, children first, suits deleting it.

r-bst-heap.text: A heap only knows its top. A balanced BST keeps the whole order: the next key in log n, a range in log n plus its length.

r-trie.text: A trie stores strings a character per level, so a lookup costs the key's length, however many keys: autocomplete, IP routing. It takes more memory.

r-binary.text: Binary search needs sorted, indexable data: twenty probes at most for a million. Its bugs: off-by-one bounds, and a midpoint sum overflowing fixed-width integers.

r-pointers.text: Two pointers walk in from both ends of a sorted array: too small, move the left; too big, move the right. Linear, not n squared.

r-window.text: A sliding window grows and shrinks one range instead of recomputing it: the longest substring without a repeat, in one pass.

r-adjacency.text: Adjacency list or matrix? Assume a million users with a hundred friends each: a list holds a hundred million entries, a matrix a trillion cells, nearly all empty. A matrix suits dense graphs and constant-time edge checks.

r-cycle.text: To find a cycle in a directed graph, run DFS marking nodes unvisited, on the path, or done. An edge back to the path is a cycle.

r-topo.text: Topological sort orders a graph with no cycles so every edge points forward, like build steps, in linear time.

r-kahn.text: Kahn's algorithm keeps removing nodes with nothing pointing in. If any are left, the graph has a cycle.

r-bits.text: And bit tricks are single instructions: take the XOR of every number, the pairs cancel, and the unpaired one is left, in constant space.
r-bits.spoken: And bit tricks are single instructions: take the ex-or of every number, the pairs cancel, and the unpaired one is left, in constant space.

close.text: None of these answers needed a line of code. The structure and the count were the argument.

next.text: And when an assistant writes the code with you, working code isn't what's graded. Next: the AI-allowed round.
